tools.name: configuration_view

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Container: rec-engine
  - ContainerPort: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed the version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.

Why this gives ~50%
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1, the Service load-balances across 4 endpoints, yielding roughly 50/50 traffic distribution.

Quick verification
- Pods:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Running
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Running
- Service Endpoints: include all 4 pods (both versions)
- Service port mapping unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Notes and adjustments
- To shift canary weight, change replica counts (e.g., canary 1, stable 3 ≈ 25% canary).
- Rollback: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 and optionally scale down or delete engine-v2-1.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Container: rec-engine
  - ContainerPort: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed the version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.

Why this gives ~50%
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1, the Service load-balances across 4 endpoints, yielding roughly 50/50 traffic distribution.

Quick verification
- Pods:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Running
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Running
- Service Endpoints: include all 4 pods (both versions)
- Service port mapping unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Notes and adjustments
- To shift canary weight, change replica counts (e.g., canary 1, stable 3 ≈ 25% canary).
- Rollback: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 and optionally scale down or delete engine-v2-1.

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Container: rec-engine
  - ContainerPort: 80 (matching stable)
  - Security configuration: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed the version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.

Why this gives ~50%
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1, the Service load-balances across 4 endpoints, yielding roughly 50/50 traffic distribution.

Quick verification
- Pods:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Running
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Running
- Service Endpoints: include all 4 pods (both versions)
- Service port mapping unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Notes and adjustments
- To shift canary weight, change replica counts (e.g., canary 1, stable 3 ≈ 25% canary).
- Rollback: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 and optionally scale down or delete engine-v2-1.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff.

- Updated the app Deployment in crashloop-test to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  - args: ["nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]
  - Left the image as quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged

Current status
- Deployment app (generation 2) is Available and Progressing = True.
- 1/1 replicas ready.
- Pod app-7f77dddbf8-n5lvt is Running.

If you’d prefer using the image’s default entrypoint instead, I can remove command/args entirely.

Steps.message:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Updated the app Deployment in crashloop-test to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  - args: ["nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]
  - Left the image as quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged

Current status
- Deployment app (generation 2) is Available and Progressing = True.
- 1/1 replicas ready.
- Pod app-7f77dddbf8-n5lvt is Running.

If you’d prefer using the image’s default entrypoint instead, I can remove command/args entirely.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Updated the app Deployment in crashloop-test to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  - args: ["nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]
  - Left the image as quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged

Current status
- Deployment app (generation 2) is Available and Progressing = True.
- 1/1 replicas ready.
- Pod app-7f77dddbf8-n5lvt is Running.

If you’d prefer using the image’s default entrypoint instead, I can remove command/args entirely.

Done.

- Root cause: The Deployment was using a non-existent image tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag), causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.
- Fix applied: Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a valid image: docker.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine.
- Result: A new ReplicaSet was created and the new Pod is running:
  - Pod: app-96469c9-pkt6g — Ready 1/1, Status: Running
  - The old failing Pod is terminating.

If you prefer a different registry/tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine or nginx:stable), tell me and I’ll switch it.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the root cause.

What was wrong
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which specified storageClassName: sc.
- StorageClass sc didn’t exist, so the PVC was Pending, which kept the pod Unschedulable.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath) so the PVC could be dynamically provisioned.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound to PV pvc-2e95dae2-e2b7-4e11-b310-3dc261f52b7a (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (pod IP 10.244.0.22).

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc”), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found and fixed the root cause.

What was wrong
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which specified storageClassName: sc.
- StorageClass sc didn’t exist, so the PVC was Pending, which kept the pod Unschedulable.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath) so the PVC could be dynamically provisioned.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound to PV pvc-2e95dae2-e2b7-4e11-b310-3dc261f52b7a (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (pod IP 10.244.0.22).

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc”), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the root cause.

What was wrong
- The pod mounts PVC homepage-pvc, which specified storageClassName: sc.
- StorageClass sc didn’t exist, so the PVC was Pending, which kept the pod Unschedulable.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath) so the PVC could be dynamically provisioned.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound to PV pvc-2e95dae2-e2b7-4e11-b310-3dc261f52b7a (1Gi, RWO).
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster (pod IP 10.244.0.22).

If you intended to use a different StorageClass (e.g., “standard” or “csi-hostpath-sc”), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent paths and the wrong port:
  - Liveness: GET http://:80/get_status
  - Readiness: GET http://:80/is_ready
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 by default and serves on “/”, so the probes failed, the pod never became Ready, and the Service had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as well; harmless).
- Updated the Service:
  - Kept service port at 80 for clients.
  - Set targetPort to 8080 so it forwards to the container’s actual listening port.

Current status

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent paths and the wrong port:
  - Liveness: GET http://:80/get_status
  - Readiness: GET http://:80/is_ready
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 by default and serves on “/”, so the probes failed, the pod never became Ready, and the Service had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as well; harmless).
- Updated the Service:
  - Kept service port at 80 for clients.
  - Set targetPort to 8080 so it forwards to the container’s actual listening port.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-qkszz).
- Service endpoints: populated (e.g., 10.244.0.25:8080).
- Health checks passing; HTTP returns 200 OK internally.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods
- kubectl -n orders get endpoints webapp
- From inside the cluster: curl -sI http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ | head -1 → should be “HTTP/1.1 200 OK”

Optional next step
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. If you need external access, tell me the hostname (or that you want a NodePort), and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent paths and the wrong port:
  - Liveness: GET http://:80/get_status
  - Readiness: GET http://:80/is_ready
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 by default and serves on “/”, so the probes failed, the pod never became Ready, and the Service had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as well; harmless).
- Updated the Service:
  - Kept service port at 80 for clients.
  - Set targetPort to 8080 so it forwards to the container’s actual listening port.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5fb688dc88-qkszz).
- Service endpoints: populated (e.g., 10.244.0.25:8080).
- Health checks passing; HTTP returns 200 OK internally.

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods
- kubectl -n orders get endpoints webapp
- From inside the cluster: curl -sI http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ | head -1 → should be “HTTP/1.1 200 OK”

Optional next step
- There is no Ingress/Route configured. If you need external access, tell me the hostname (or that you want a NodePort), and I’ll set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The nginx Deployment runs image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on port 8080 (not 80). Verified inside the pod:
  - curl 127.0.0.1:80 → connection refused
  - curl 127.0.0.1:8080 → HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- The Service web/nginx had:
  - selector: app=web (but the pods are labeled app=nginx)
  - targetPort: 80 (but the container listens on 8080)
- Because of the selector mismatch, the Service had no endpoints; even after fixing the selector, targetPort would still have been wrong.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: 80 → targetPort: 8080
- Kept the existing ClusterIP. Result:
  - Endpoints now show the nginx pod IP on port 8080.
  - curl to the Service ClusterIP:80 returns HTTP 200 from nginx.

What I verified
- Endpoints: now populated with the pod and port 8080.
- In-pod test: curl -I http://10.101.193.197:80 → HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

How you can validate
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -I http://nginx
  or from any pod in the cluster: curl -I http://10.101.193.197

Notes
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - Or create an Ingress (recommended with an Ingress controller) pointing to svc nginx port 80.

Root cause summary
- Mismatched Service selector (app=web vs app=nginx) and incorrect targetPort (80 vs 8080) prevented endpoints from being created and traffic from reaching the pod. Both issues are now corrected.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The nginx Deployment runs image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on port 8080 (not 80). Verified inside the pod:
  - curl 127.0.0.1:80 → connection refused
  - curl 127.0.0.1:8080 → HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- The Service web/nginx had:
  - selector: app=web (but the pods are labeled app=nginx)
  - targetPort: 80 (but the container listens on 8080)
- Because of the selector mismatch, the Service had no endpoints; even after fixing the selector, targetPort would still have been wrong.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: 80 → targetPort: 8080
- Kept the existing ClusterIP. Result:
  - Endpoints now show the nginx pod IP on port 8080.
  - curl to the Service ClusterIP:80 returns HTTP 200 from nginx.

What I verified
- Endpoints: now populated with the pod and port 8080.
- In-pod test: curl -I http://10.101.193.197:80 → HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

How you can validate
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -I http://nginx
  or from any pod in the cluster: curl -I http://10.101.193.197

Notes
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - Or create an Ingress (recommended with an Ingress controller) pointing to svc nginx port 80.

Root cause summary
- Mismatched Service selector (app=web vs app=nginx) and incorrect targetPort (80 vs 8080) prevented endpoints from being created and traffic from reaching the pod. Both issues are now corrected.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The nginx Deployment runs image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on port 8080 (not 80). Verified inside the pod:
  - curl 127.0.0.1:80 → connection refused
  - curl 127.0.0.1:8080 → HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- The Service web/nginx had:
  - selector: app=web (but the pods are labeled app=nginx)
  - targetPort: 80 (but the container listens on 8080)
- Because of the selector mismatch, the Service had no endpoints; even after fixing the selector, targetPort would still have been wrong.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: 80 → targetPort: 8080
- Kept the existing ClusterIP. Result:
  - Endpoints now show the nginx pod IP on port 8080.
  - curl to the Service ClusterIP:80 returns HTTP 200 from nginx.

What I verified
- Endpoints: now populated with the pod and port 8080.
- In-pod test: curl -I http://10.101.193.197:80 → HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

How you can validate
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -I http://nginx
  or from any pod in the cluster: curl -I http://10.101.193.197

Notes
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - Or create an Ingress (recommended with an Ingress controller) pointing to svc nginx port 80.

Root cause summary
- Mismatched Service selector (app=web vs app=nginx) and incorrect targetPort (80 vs 8080) prevented endpoints from being created and traffic from reaching the pod. Both issues are now corrected.

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label.
- The Service web-app-service existed and selected app=web-app, but with no running pods it had no endpoints. Connecting to a ClusterIP with no endpoints returns connection refused, which matches your frontend error.

Fix applied
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result: Deployment web-app-deployment rolled out a new ReplicaSet and now has 2/2 pods Ready and Available. The new pods are running on node mcp-eval-cluster, and the Service’s selector matches them, so endpoints are now populated.

Why this resolves the error
- With pods running behind the Service, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will be routed correctly instead of being refused due to empty endpoints.

Verification you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy web-app-deployment
  Expect: READY 2/2, AVAILABLE 2
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -l app=web-app -o wide
  Expect: pods Running with IPs
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-app-service
  Expect: addresses listing the pod IPs
- Optional in-cluster test: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- /bin/sh
  Then: wget -qO- http://web-app-service

Notes and follow-ups
- If you intended to target special nodes (e.g., GPU), either:
  - Add the correct label to those nodes (kubectl label node <name> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Reintroduce a nodeSelector/tolerations that match actual node labels.
- Consider adding readinessProbe and livenessProbe to the container so the Service won’t send traffic until the app is ready. Example readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label.
- The Service web-app-service existed and selected app=web-app, but with no running pods it had no endpoints. Connecting to a ClusterIP with no endpoints returns connection refused, which matches your frontend error.

Fix applied
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result: Deployment web-app-deployment rolled out a new ReplicaSet and now has 2/2 pods Ready and Available. The new pods are running on node mcp-eval-cluster, and the Service’s selector matches them, so endpoints are now populated.

Why this resolves the error
- With pods running behind the Service, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will be routed correctly instead of being refused due to empty endpoints.

Verification you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy web-app-deployment
  Expect: READY 2/2, AVAILABLE 2
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -l app=web-app -o wide
  Expect: pods Running with IPs
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-app-service
  Expect: addresses listing the pod IPs
- Optional in-cluster test: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- /bin/sh
  Then: wget -qO- http://web-app-service

Notes and follow-ups
- If you intended to target special nodes (e.g., GPU), either:
  - Add the correct label to those nodes (kubectl label node <name> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Reintroduce a nodeSelector/tolerations that match actual node labels.
- Consider adding readinessProbe and livenessProbe to the container so the Service won’t send traffic until the app is ready. Example readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.” The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no node with that label.
- The Service web-app-service existed and selected app=web-app, but with no running pods it had no endpoints. Connecting to a ClusterIP with no endpoints returns connection refused, which matches your frontend error.

Fix applied
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on the available node.
- Result: Deployment web-app-deployment rolled out a new ReplicaSet and now has 2/2 pods Ready and Available. The new pods are running on node mcp-eval-cluster, and the Service’s selector matches them, so endpoints are now populated.

Why this resolves the error
- With pods running behind the Service, connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 will be routed correctly instead of being refused due to empty endpoints.

Verification you can run
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy web-app-deployment
  Expect: READY 2/2, AVAILABLE 2
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -l app=web-app -o wide
  Expect: pods Running with IPs
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-app-service
  Expect: addresses listing the pod IPs
- Optional in-cluster test: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- /bin/sh
  Then: wget -qO- http://web-app-service

Notes and follow-ups
- If you intended to target special nodes (e.g., GPU), either:
  - Add the correct label to those nodes (kubectl label node <name> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Reintroduce a nodeSelector/tolerations that match actual node labels.
- Consider adding readinessProbe and livenessProbe to the container so the Service won’t send traffic until the app is ready. Example readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80.

outputSteps.content:
Done. communication-pod is running in multi-container-logging with the requested setup.

What I deployed
- Pod: communication-pod (namespace: multi-container-logging)
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    - Exposes containerPort 8080
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (pod is Ready when the web server serves traffic)
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox:latest
    - Command: tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log

Notes
- fsGroup is set to 101 so nginx (runs as UID/GID 101) can write logs to the shared volume.

How to verify
- Check pod status:
  kubectl get pod communication-pod -n multi-container-logging
- Generate traffic and see logs:
  kubectl port-forward pod/communication-pod 8080:8080 -n multi-container-logging
  curl -s localhost:8080 >/dev/null
  kubectl logs communication-pod -c logger -n multi-container-logging --tail=20

If you want the exact manifest I applied, say “show manifest” and I’ll paste it.

Done.

What I changed
- Identified that storage-pod mounts PVC storage-pvc in the resize-pv namespace.
- Verified the StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc supports expansion.
- Resized the PVC request from 1Gi to 3Gi.
- Restarted the pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node (brief interruption).

Current state
- PVC storage-pvc:
  - Requested: 3Gi
  - Capacity: 3Gi
  - Phase: Bound
- PV bound to the PVC shows capacity 3Gi.
- Pod storage-pod is Running and reattached to the PVC.

Notes
- With the hostpath CSI driver, filesystem-mode volumes are directories on the node. Inside the container, df may show the node’s root filesystem capacity rather than “3Gi”. The authoritative size is in the PVC status.

How to verify
- kubectl get pvc storage-pvc -n resize-pv -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}{"\n"}'
  Expected output: 3Gi
- kubectl describe pvc storage-pvc -n resize-pv
  Check that Capacity is 3Gi and there are no pending resize conditions.

What I changed
- Identified that storage-pod mounts PVC storage-pvc in the resize-pv namespace.
- Verified the StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc supports expansion.
- Resized the PVC request from 1Gi to 3Gi.
- Restarted the pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node (brief interruption).

- PVC storage-pvc:
  - Requested: 3Gi
  - Capacity: 3Gi
  - Phase: Bound
- PV bound to the PVC shows capacity 3Gi.
- Pod storage-pod is Running and reattached to the PVC.

Notes
- With the hostpath CSI driver, filesystem-mode volumes are directories on the node. Inside the container, df may show the node’s root filesystem capacity rather than “3Gi”. The authoritative size is in the PVC status.

How to verify
- kubectl get pvc storage-pvc -n resize-pv -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}{"\n"}'
  Expected output: 3Gi
- kubectl describe pvc storage-pvc -n resize-pv
  Check that Capacity is 3Gi and there are no pending resize conditions.

outputSteps.content:
Done.

What I changed
- Identified that storage-pod mounts PVC storage-pvc in the resize-pv namespace.
- Verified the StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc supports expansion.
- Resized the PVC request from 1Gi to 3Gi.
- Restarted the pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node (brief interruption).

Current state
- PVC storage-pvc:
  - Requested: 3Gi
  - Capacity: 3Gi
  - Phase: Bound
- PV bound to the PVC shows capacity 3Gi.
- Pod storage-pod is Running and reattached to the PVC.

Notes
- With the hostpath CSI driver, filesystem-mode volumes are directories on the node. Inside the container, df may show the node’s root filesystem capacity rather than “3Gi”. The authoritative size is in the PVC status.

How to verify
- kubectl get pvc storage-pvc -n resize-pv -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}{"\n"}'
  Expected output: 3Gi
- kubectl describe pvc storage-pvc -n resize-pv
  Check that Capacity is 3Gi and there are no pending resize conditions.

results.taskOutput:
All requested objects have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Per-developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer namespace access (least privilege)
  - Each developer user and their ServiceAccount are bound to ClusterRole edit in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: alice (User) + alice-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
    - dev-bob: bob (User) + bob-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
    - dev-charlie: charlie (User) + charlie-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
  - Rationale: edit gives full CRUD on namespaced resources without letting developers change RBAC; this satisfies “full access” to their namespace while honoring least privilege.
- dev-shared read-only
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Note: view does not allow reading Secrets.
- staging/prod restricted
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; only cluster-admins can access.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services
- dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services
- Implemented with ResourceQuota objects setting limits.cpu, limits.memory, requests.cpu, requests.memory, pods, services.

4) Network Policies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces) and explicit allows to satisfy isolation and access needs.
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - default-deny-all (Ingress + Egress)
  - allow-ingress-same-namespace (pods can talk within their own namespace)
  - allow-egress-own-shared-and-system:
    - Egress to same namespace
    - Egress to dev-shared namespace
    - Egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
  - Note: No egress to other developer namespaces; cross-developer comms are blocked.
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces:
    - From dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, and from dev-shared itself
  - allow-egress-system-and-self:
    - Egress to dev-shared (self)
    - Egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-intra-namespace:
    - Ingress from same namespace only
    - Egress to same namespace and kube-system only
  - No paths from any dev namespaces to staging/prod (isolation ensured)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, and prod.
- No changes to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system), per requirement.

Notes and next steps
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- If developers also need to read Secrets in dev-shared, replace view with a custom read-only Role that includes get on secrets, and bind that instead. Current setup intentionally withholds secrets from dev-shared to follow least privilege.
- Consider adding LimitRanges in each namespace to set sane default requests/limits so pods can be scheduled predictably under the quotas.
- ServiceAccount tokens (K8s v1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quick RBAC verification (examples):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice          => yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice              => yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice         => no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice                 => no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice                 => no

If you want, I can export all created manifests as a single multi-document YAML for version control.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested objects have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Per-developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer namespace access (least privilege)
  - Each developer user and their ServiceAccount are bound to ClusterRole edit in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: alice (User) + alice-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
    - dev-bob: bob (User) + bob-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
    - dev-charlie: charlie (User) + charlie-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
  - Rationale: edit gives full CRUD on namespaced resources without letting developers change RBAC; this satisfies “full access” to their namespace while honoring least privilege.
- dev-shared read-only
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Note: view does not allow reading Secrets.
- staging/prod restricted
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; only cluster-admins can access.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services
- dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services
- Implemented with ResourceQuota objects setting limits.cpu, limits.memory, requests.cpu, requests.memory, pods, services.

4) Network Policies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces) and explicit allows to satisfy isolation and access needs.
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - default-deny-all (Ingress + Egress)
  - allow-ingress-same-namespace (pods can talk within their own namespace)
  - allow-egress-own-shared-and-system:
    - Egress to same namespace
    - Egress to dev-shared namespace
    - Egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
  - Note: No egress to other developer namespaces; cross-developer comms are blocked.
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces:
    - From dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, and from dev-shared itself
  - allow-egress-system-and-self:
    - Egress to dev-shared (self)
    - Egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-intra-namespace:
    - Ingress from same namespace only
    - Egress to same namespace and kube-system only
  - No paths from any dev namespaces to staging/prod (isolation ensured)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, and prod.
- No changes to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system), per requirement.

Notes and next steps
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- If developers also need to read Secrets in dev-shared, replace view with a custom read-only Role that includes get on secrets, and bind that instead. Current setup intentionally withholds secrets from dev-shared to follow least privilege.
- Consider adding LimitRanges in each namespace to set sane default requests/limits so pods can be scheduled predictably under the quotas.
- ServiceAccount tokens (K8s v1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quick RBAC verification (examples):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice          => yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice              => yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice         => no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice                 => no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice                 => no

If you want, I can export all created manifests as a single multi-document YAML for version control.

outputSteps.content:
All requested objects have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces
- Per-developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer namespace access (least privilege)
  - Each developer user and their ServiceAccount are bound to ClusterRole edit in their own namespace:
    - dev-alice: alice (User) + alice-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
    - dev-bob: bob (User) + bob-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
    - dev-charlie: charlie (User) + charlie-sa (ServiceAccount) -> edit
  - Rationale: edit gives full CRUD on namespaced resources without letting developers change RBAC; this satisfies “full access” to their namespace while honoring least privilege.
- dev-shared read-only
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Note: view does not allow reading Secrets.
- staging/prod restricted
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; only cluster-admins can access.

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services
- dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services
- Implemented with ResourceQuota objects setting limits.cpu, limits.memory, requests.cpu, requests.memory, pods, services.

4) Network Policies
- Default deny everywhere (except system namespaces) and explicit allows to satisfy isolation and access needs.
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - default-deny-all (Ingress + Egress)
  - allow-ingress-same-namespace (pods can talk within their own namespace)
  - allow-egress-own-shared-and-system:
    - Egress to same namespace
    - Egress to dev-shared namespace
    - Egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
  - Note: No egress to other developer namespaces; cross-developer comms are blocked.
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces:
    - From dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, and from dev-shared itself
  - allow-egress-system-and-self:
    - Egress to dev-shared (self)
    - Egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-intra-namespace:
    - Ingress from same namespace only
    - Egress to same namespace and kube-system only
  - No paths from any dev namespaces to staging/prod (isolation ensured)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, and prod.
- No changes to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system), per requirement.

Notes and next steps
- NetworkPolicy enforcement requires a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, etc.).
- If developers also need to read Secrets in dev-shared, replace view with a custom read-only Role that includes get on secrets, and bind that instead. Current setup intentionally withholds secrets from dev-shared to follow least privilege.
- Consider adding LimitRanges in each namespace to set sane default requests/limits so pods can be scheduled predictably under the quotas.
- ServiceAccount tokens (K8s v1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quick RBAC verification (examples):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice          => yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice              => yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice         => no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice                 => no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice                 => no

If you want, I can export all created manifests as a single multi-document YAML for version control.

Done.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP None) for stable network IDs
- StatefulSet: db
  - Replicas: initially 3
  - Each pod mounts a 1Gi PVC at /data
  - initContainer writes initial_data to /data/test on first start
  - Container: busybox sleeping to keep pod running

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica. The desired replicas are now 1; the cluster may take a moment to terminate the extra pods.

How to verify (optional)
- kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db
- kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- cat /data/test  # should output: initial_data

Notes
- Each pod has its own PVC (data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2). Scaling down retains the PVCs so data persists. A default StorageClass must exist for dynamic provisioning.

- Namespace: statefulset-test

  - Replicas: initially 3

- kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- cat /data/test  # should output: initial_data

- Each pod has its own PVC (data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2). Scaling down retains the PVCs so data persists. A default StorageClass must exist for dynamic provisioning.
